title: Paradise Airlines 901A
summary: Paradise Airlines Flight 901A, a Lockheed L-049 Constellation operating from Oakland to Lake Tahoe, crashed on March 1, 1964, during a heavy snowstorm near Genoa Peak on the eastern side of Lake Tahoe. The aircraft encountered icing conditions at altitude and deteriorating visibility as it approached the destination. The pilot reported seeing a break in cloud cover and the airport, then proceeded with a visual approach despite weather unsuitable for visual flying. The aircraft lost altitude awareness and spatial orientation in the poor visibility and fell below minimum safe altitude in the mountainous terrain. The aircraft crashed into the mountain, killing all 85 passengers and crew aboard. At the time, this was the second-deadliest single-aircraft crash in U.S. history.
probable_cause: Pilot decision to conduct visual approach during weather conditions requiring instrument flight rules, loss of altitude awareness and spatial disorientation in clouds and snow, descent below minimum safe altitude, and controlled flight into terrain.

factors.evidence: Icing conditions at 12,000 feet degraded aircraft performance
Snow showers and clouds obscured visual references
False visual perception of airport through cloud break
Crew lost altitude and position awareness in clouds
Aircraft descended below minimum safe altitude in mountainous terrain
Aircraft struck mountain at low altitude

events.text: Flight 901A departed San Jose at 10:39 PST for 50-minute flight to Lake Tahoe
En route, crew reported icing conditions at 12,000 feet and snow showers over Lake Tahoe
Pilot reported seeing break in clouds and airport on south shore, proceeded with visual approach
Aircraft lost altitude awareness in poor visibility
Aircraft crashed near Genoa Peak at Lake Tahoe in heavy snowstorm

title: United Airlines 823
summary: United Airlines Flight 823, a Vickers Viscount operating from Philadelphia to Huntsville, Alabama, experienced an uncontrollable in-flight fire of undetermined origin in the passenger cabin on July 9, 1964. The fire resulted in rapid loss of control of the aircraft. One passenger attempted to exit through window but did not survive the free-fall. The aircraft crashed 2.25 miles northeast of Parrottsville, Tennessee, killing all 39 aboard. Investigation could not identify the source of fuel, ignition point, or cause of the final maneuver.
probable_cause: Uncontrollable in-flight fire of undetermined origin in the fuselage, resulting in loss of control of the aircraft. The source of fuel and ignition point could not be identified from the accident investigation.

factors.evidence: Uncontrollable in-flight fire occurred in passenger cabin
Aircraft lost control due to fire damage and effects
Post-impact fire destroyed evidence and structures

events.text: Uncontrollable in-flight fire of undetermined origin occurred in passenger cabin
Aircraft crashed 2.25 miles northeast of Parrottsville Tennessee, all 39 aboard killed

title: TWA 800
summary: Trans World Airlines Flight 800, a Boeing 707, suffered a rejected takeoff at Rome Fiumicino Airport when instruments indicated engine failure. During the rejected takeoff, the number 2 engine thrust reverser failed to engage properly, causing asymmetrical thrust that prevented normal deceleration. The aircraft overran the runway and struck ground equipment, igniting a right-wing fuel leak. Multiple fuel tank explosions followed, destroying the aircraft and killing 49 of 73 aboard.
probable_cause: Inoperative number 2 engine reverse thrust system caused by disconnection of a pneumatic duct actuating mechanism. The resulting forward thrust from engine 2 despite reverse position created asymmetrical thrust, preventing aircraft from stopping within the available runway distance.

factors.evidence: Engine number 4 instruments indicated zero thrust at 80 knots during takeoff roll
Reverser Unlock light illuminated for engine number 2, indicating uncommanded reverse thrust deployment
Disconnected pneumatic duct failed to maintain pressure for clamshell door actuator
Aircraft overran declared runway end and struck ground equipment
Wing tanks leaked fuel from damage sustained during runway impact
Center fuel tank and number 1 fuel tank explosions occurred post-impact
Fire destroyed aircraft and blocked evacuation routes
